messages.subject: get.real() combining sex specifice densities and se's
messages.subject_clean: get.real() combining sex specifice densities and se's
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

 Using the get.real() function for a multisession sex-specific model is there an easy way to make it combine the density estimates and se's for both sexes within a session? Essentially I'm looking for total density per session with standard errors.

Best,

David

messages.subject: Get.real
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

First, what a great function name- get.real().

I am projecting density from an oscr model across western North America. I have about 4.3M cells of interest. For some reason get.real seems slow to predict, it took ~6 mins to predict on 100 rows, so extrapolating to 4.3M rows, it will take a very long time (I think >100 days..). Is this expected behaviour? Should I do something different, or is there a bug on my end?

Cheers,
Clayton

--
Clayton Lamb, PhD
Postdoctoral Researcher
Universities of British Columbia & Montana

messages.subject: RE: [oscr] Get.real
messages.body_plain:
Hi Clayton,

Just to add to Dan’s comment:

I just went through this process for projections across New Hampshire. Turns out that for a given model, times scales pretty linearly with number of pixels. If you need maps of uncertainty, then it’s going to be time consuming unless you coarsen the resolution of the prediction raster or parallelize the whole thing. If you want a map of expected density, then you can compute that by hand (the time consuming part of get.real() is the computing the se using the delta method). Similar thing happens when projecting across large spaces using models in unmarked.

messages.subject: RE: [oscr] Get.real
messages.body_plain:
I actually think you want the following:

#say spdf is the data frame of pixel values for the whole area

ED <- exp(d.0 + d.beta.hii_log *    spdf$hii_log +

                d.beta.ndvi_scale * spdf$ndvi_scale +

                d.beta.cc_scale *   spdf$cc_scale)

Probably worth adding a se=F argument for get.real().

messages.subject: Re: [oscr] Converting scrFrame and ssDF units
messages.body_plain:
The short answer is that you don't have to change the telemetry object.  The relative frequencies per cell are the same, regardless of coordinate system.

The pixel frequencies are calculated based on the telemetry XY coordinates and the state space XY coordinates.  Whether those coordinates are meters or km does not matter, they just have to be the same at the moment the frequencies are tallied.

The purpose of scaling is generally to reduce distance calculations and the coefficient size of sigma to help the function maximize the likelihood.  This is partially referenced on page 155 of the SCR book, though in regards to the mixing of MCMC chains (the concept is somewhat similar).  In that example, Andy scaled the state space so that 1 unit of distance was 10km and, therefore, the log-scale sigma estimate was multiplied by 10 after exponentiation to get km.

It's important to keep track of your spatial scaling and understand what it means throughout your workflow with these models.  The intercept gives you the log-scale density of a pixel, but your "pixel" can be any size as defined by your state space.

messages.subject: RE: [oscr] Converting scrFrame and ssDF units
messages.body_plain:
Just to add to Dan’s helpful comments.

We had in mind that users would build oSCR data objects (scrFrame, ssDF) once at the beginning an analysis so as to have all the sausage making happen *prior to* the analytical workflow. This is mostly for transparency sake but also makes reading/reviewing/sharing scripts much easier (in my opinion), and minimizes the need to edit oSCR objects (these have a specific and relational structure).

So, with that said, my preference here would be to have a pre-oSCR data manipulation step that divides the coordinates in the tdf and the telemetry object, and then create the oSCR objects. This way, you guarantee everything from data2oscr() forward is correctly formatted.

Chris
